extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, and researchers doing proofs and research-level writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and formulating individual claims, lemmas, computations, and larger research goals so they are purposeful, necessary, and feasible. Applies to small claims up to broad research programs and to writing lemmas in papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle — maintain vision
rubrics_metrics.description: "Worse than being blind, is to see and have no vision." — Helen Keller. Pause regularly to recall why you're pursuing a goal, not just what you're doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodically step back from technical work to reconnect with the underlying goal or motivation (at the level of computations, lemmas, theorems, or career aims). Use this to avoid aimless work and to ensure effort aligns with broader objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the lemma were proven, how would it be used?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proving or writing a lemma, identify its precise role in the argument or project. Specify downstream uses (which steps or results rely on it) so the lemma isn't incidental machinery. This helps decide whether the lemma is necessary and how to present it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance
rubrics_metrics.description: "What features of the lemma are most important for you?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which aspects (strength of statement, specific hypotheses, quantitative bounds, generality) genuinely matter for later steps. Emphasize those features in the statement and proof; deemphasize or remove irrelevant technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization (minimal sufficient result)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a weaker/less precise statement would still enable the later argument. If so, prefer the weaker but simpler lemma to reduce proof complexity and increase clarity. This avoids overworking for unnecessary strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (simplicity of formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Is there a simpler formulation of the lemma?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the simplest clean statement that captures what's needed. A simpler formulation improves readability and helps readers (and you) see why the lemma matters. Consider rephrasing, changing notation, or isolating the core idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility (worth vs difficulty of hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Is it worth trying to omit a hypothesis of the lemma, if that hypothesis seems hard to obtain?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the cost of proving a stronger version (by removing hypotheses) against the benefit to the project. If omitting a hypothesis is difficult and not essential, accept the stronger hypothesis; otherwise, attempt to weaken only if payoff justifies effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of application
rubrics_metrics.description: These questions apply across scales: small tasks (claims, computations), medium work (proving lemmas), large projects (theorems, research programs, career goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same checklist at all levels of mathematical work: micro-level (individual computations), meso-level (lemmas in a paper), and macro-level (research direction, career planning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good lemma communicates purpose and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A "good" lemma in a paper is one where the author has already answered these five questions; the reader feels purpose and necessity rather than incidental machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, make the lemma's purpose, important features, minimal needed strength, simple formulation, and feasible hypotheses explicit (via statement, remark, or surrounding text) so readers immediately grasp why the lemma exists and how it's used.
